subject: Critical Thinking
title: Digital Citizenship: Sharing Responsibly in a Connected World
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Digital Citizenship: Sharing Responsibly in a Connected World.

hook.text: You share a false story. Your 500 friends share it. Each of their friends shares it.

buildup.text: Every share is an implicit endorsement.

discovery.text: Digital citizenship: using technology responsibly, ethically, and with awareness of its impact on others and society.

twist.text: The most effective misinformation fighters aren't fact-checkers — they're ordinary people who pause before sharing.

climax.text: Before sharing: Is it true? Is the source credible? Is it helpful? Could it cause harm? If unsure, don't share.

punchline.text: The share button is a broadcast tool. Use it like one.

quiz.question: What is the most effective way ordinary people can combat misinformation?
options: Pausing to verify claims before sharing them

details.summary: Digital citizenship means taking responsibility for the information you amplify online. Every share, retweet, and forward is an act of publishing, and responsible sharing requires the same standards you would want others to apply.
details.whyItMatters: In a connected world, everyone is a publisher. Irresponsible sharing amplifies misinformation, damages reputations, and erodes the information ecosystem that democracy depends on.
takeaways: Sharing is publishing — treat it with the same responsibility
Verify before you amplify any claim or story
Model the information behavior you want to see in others

faq.question: What responsibility do individual social media users have for shared content?
faq.answer: When you share misinformation, you lend it your credibility and extend its reach. Even if you did not create it, sharing amplifies it. Treating each share as a personal endorsement raises your standard and reduces the spread of false information.

faq.question: How can you correct yourself publicly if you have shared misinformation?
faq.answer: Delete the original post if possible, create a visible correction explaining what was wrong and what the accurate information is, and resist the temptation to minimize. Transparent self-correction models good information behavior and strengthens your credibility.
